And whoever says one hundred times, "Glory be to Allah, and praise be to Allah, and I seek the forgiveness of Allah, and there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest, and as Allah wills, and there is no might nor power except in Allah; Allah is sufficient for me, I have taken refuge in Allah, I have relied upon Allah."

None knows what reward such a person has with God, whose name be exalted, save God alone; and the least of it is ten thousand good deeds, for God multiplies a single good deed tenfold, as He has said. It is recommended that whoever rises from the prayer, on leaving it, utter the takbir three times and then say: "There is no god but God, alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the kingdom and to Him belongs praise; in His hand is all good, and He is able to do all things. There is no god but God alone; He fulfilled His promise, gave victory to His servant, and defeated the confederates alone; to Him belongs the kingdom and to Him belongs praise. Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds. There is no god but God, and God is greatest; glory be to God, and praise be to God." This is said ten times.

Ali (ع) used to say after every prescribed prayer: "Then by Your light You guided, so to You belongs praise; Your forbearance is great, so You pardoned, and to You belongs praise; You stretched out Your hands and gave, so to You belongs praise. Our Lord, Your face is the most generous of faces, Your station the best of stations, and Your gift the most beneficial and the most pleasant of gifts. You are obeyed, our Lord, and You give thanks; You are disobeyed, our Lord, and You forgive. You answer the supplication of the distressed, heal the sick, and deliver from affliction. Our Lord, You accept repentance and forgive sins for whom You will; none can requite Your favor, and no speaker can number Your due." Abu Abd Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said: "Because this is a remembrance of God as He deserves to be remembered a thousandfold, whoever says it will have a thousand good deeds."

It is right and recommended, too, to say after the prayer: "O God, for You I have prayed, to You I have called, and in You I have hoped; so I ask You to place in my prayer and my supplication a blessing by which You expiate my sins, whiten my face, honor my standing, and lift my burden from me. O God, put down my burden, and make what is with You better for me. Praise be to God, who has discharged from me a prayer that was ordained upon me and upon the believers as a timed obligation." And Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (ع) said: "The least that will suffice you in supplication after the obligatory prayer is to say: O God, I ask You for every good that Your knowledge encompasses, and I seek refuge in You from every evil that Your knowledge encompasses. O God, I ask You for well-being in all my affairs, and I seek refuge in You from the disgrace of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter."

### The desirable forms of supplication

There is no appointed time for supplication. Whoever wishes to pray may do so, asking God for his needs and calling upon Him for whatever he loves, so long as he does not call for a wrong or for the severing of kinship. It is fitting for one who would supplicate that he set a righteous deed before his supplication, that he repent to God of his sins, that he clear himself of the claims standing between him and others of God's creation, and that he make his deed and his intention sincerely for God. For it is related of the Messenger of God (ص) that he said: "One who supplicates without action is like one who draws a bow without a string." And Abu Dharr (رضي الله عنه) said: "Righteous conduct is sufficient accompaniment for supplication, as salt is sufficient seasoning for food."

Whoever would supplicate should begin by praising God his Lord and extolling Him as He deserves, and by blessing Muhammad His prophet and his family; then let him make his petition, and let him bless the prophet and his family in the middle of his supplication and at its end. For the Messenger of God (ص) heard a man supplicating before he had praised God, and said: "This man has been hasty with his Lord." And when he wished to supplicate he would begin by praising God, then say: "O God, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none who can give what You withhold; none who can constrain what You expand, and none who can expand what You constrain; none who can bring forward what You defer, and none who can defer what You bring forward. O God, You are the Forbearing, so You are never rash; You are the Bountiful, so You are never niggardly; You are the Mighty, so You are never abased; You are the Impregnable, so You are never assailed; You are the Possessor of Majesty and Honor; and there is no power and no strength save in God, the Most High, the Almighty."

He also said: "Do not make me like the rider's cup." For the rider fills his cup and sets it aside, and when he has finished with his gear and his need he looks: if he has need to drink he drinks, or if he has need to make ablution he makes ablution, and otherwise he pours it out. "Place me at the beginning of the supplication, and in the middle of the supplication, and at the end of the supplication." He meant by this that the blessing upon him and his family should not stand at the end of the supplication only, but should stand at its beginning, its middle, and its end.

When God sent down the verse commanding the believers to bless the prophet, the people said: "O Messenger of God, you have taught us how to greet you; how, then, are we to bless you?" He said: "Say: O God, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

> فَمَا ٱسْتَكَانُوا۟ لِرَبِّهِمْ وَمَا يَتَضَرَّعُونَ

Ali (ع) was asked about the saying of God, ﴾فَمَا اسْتَكَانُوا لِرَبِّهِمْ وَمَا يَتَضَرَّعُونَ﴿, "They did not humble themselves to their Lord, nor did they supplicate" (al-Muminun: 76). He said: "They were not lowly in their supplication to God, nor were they sincere in it."

Supplications are more than can be numbered or contained in a book, yet we mention some of that whose answering may be hoped for, as it has come to us from the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), from the reports and the encouragement to it. Among this is what was related of the Messenger of God (ص), that he said: "There are ninety-nine names; whoever numbers them enters Paradise." This tradition has been narrated often, and men have differed over these names and been at sea concerning them. Sufyan al-Thawri set them down in his compendium, and named names other than those handed down from the Imams (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), naming them at variance with what they gave. Ali ibn al-Husayn (ع) was asked about them, and he described their excellence and the answering of the supplication of whoever prays by them, and magnified their standing in words too long to relate. He took a covenant of whoever learned them of him that he would teach them only to one he trusted, and would not supplicate God by them for any wrong or for the severing of His kinship. He said that they are in the Book of God, whose mention is exalted.

In the Opening of the Book are five names: By God, O Lord, O Most Merciful, O Ever Compassionate, O King. In Surah al-Baqarah are twenty-six: O Encompassing, O All-Powerful, O All-Knowing, O Wise, O Ever-Relenting, O Patient, O Vast, O Originator, O Hearing, O Sufficient, O Knowing, O Kind, O Grateful, O God, O One, O Forgiving, O Forbearing, O Withholder, O Expander, O Living, O Self-Subsisting, O Most High, O Great, O Rich, O Guardian, O Praiseworthy. In Surah Al Imran are four: O Ever-Standing, O Bestower, O Swift in Reckoning, O Aware. In Surah al-Nisa: O Watchful, O Witness, O Pardoning, O Nourisher, O Trustee. In Surah al-Anam are five: O Fashioner, O Subduer, O Able, O Subtle, O Ruler. In Surah al-Araf are two: O Giver of Life, O Giver of Death. In Surah al-Anfal are two: O Best of Protectors, O Best of Helpers. In Surah Hud are seven: O Preserver, O Near, O Answerer, O Strong, O Glorious, O Loving, O Doer of what He wills. In Surah al-Ra'd are two: O Great, O Most Exalted. In Surah Ibrahim is one: O Ever-Giving. In Surah al-Hujurat is one: O Ever-Creating. In Surah al-Hajj is one: O Raiser of the dead. In Surah al-Anbiya are two: O Truthful, O Inheritor. In Surah al-Muminun is one: O Generous. In Surah al-Nur: O Guide. In Surah Saba is one: O Opener. In Surah al-Mumin are four: O Forgiver, O Accepter of repentance, O Severe in punishment, O Possessor of Bounty. In Surah al-Dhariyat are three: O Provider, O Possessor of Strength, O Firm. In Surah al-Tur is one: O Ever-Kind. In Surah Iqtarabat is one: O Omnipotent. In Surah al-Rahman are three: O Everlasting, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor. In Surah al-Hadid are four: O First, O Last, O Manifest, O Hidden. In Surah al-Hashr are ten: O Holy, O Peace, O Granter of Security, O Overseer, O Mighty, O Compeller, O Supreme, O Creator, O Maker, O Fashioner. In Surah al-Buruj are two: O Beginner, O Restorer. In Surah al-Ikhlas are two: O One, O Eternal Refuge.

These are the names of God, exalted is His mention, in His Book: ninety-nine names, and with "By God" a hundred. By them, when God is called upon He answers, and when He is asked He gives. A company of the believers who prayed by them with sincerity and certainty have known the blessing of their being answered; their mention is attested and their excellence handed down.

> إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّلِحَتِ سَيَجْعَلُ لَهُمُ ٱلرَّحْمَنُ وُدًّۭا

The Messenger of God (ص) said to Ali (ع): "O Ali, shall I not teach you words which, were your sins upon you like the foam of the sea, God would put away from you? Say: O God, fix for me affection in the breasts of the believers, and make for me with You a covenant," or, "make for me with You affection." Then God sent down: ﴾إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ سَيَجْعَلُ لَهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ وُدًّا﴿, "Verily those who believe and do righteous deeds, the All-Merciful will appoint for them affection" (Maryam: 96). And this was among the supplications recited concerning him (ع).

There was a supplication of Ali (ع), the supreme supplication of the Imams, by which he would pray in weighty matters. He would say: O God, I seek from You the grace to thank You well; I ask of You the gift of a tongue unloosed in proclaiming Your praise; and I desire from You to be set right in what earns Your increase. I seek refuge in You from that which calls down the visitation of other than You and brings on the sudden strokes that befall the like of me. O God, You began with me by the most abundant of gifts and singled me out for them above much of Your creation, so that, without my asking, there fell to me from Your apportioning the most fortunate share and the fullest lot, when You made me among the people of Your knowledge and those who hold fast to the rope of Your oneness, before the passing of ages, the elapsing of times, and the running of the eras, before the creation of male and female, the multiplying of generations, and the succession of descendants. Then You created me in the finest form and the most complete image, and made me hearing, seeing, speaking, understanding, discerning. Then You set my frame straight and completed my faculties, and did not deprive me of any of my limbs, but fortified them against afflictions by Your power and kept them from the stillness of incapacity by Your governance. As You have taken it upon Yourself, O my God, to repel maladies from my body by my health and to guard my weakness, so bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You are worthy and as they are worthy of You. Remove from my soul the hindrance of sloth and the discouragement of delay; release it from the grip of weariness and loose from it the fetters of listlessness; rouse it to bear the burdens with which You have charged it, and set it upon the bounds of Your sacred limits.

O God, loose my tongue with the abundance of Your remembrance, the goodness of thanking You, and the repeating of Your favors; make it flourish with the recitation of Your Book at every hour of night and day; make it prefer truth in hope of its benefit and forsake falsehood in fear of its harm; restrain it from sharing in the backbiting of the backbiters and from chewing over the honor of the believers; and silence it from the stabbing of slanderers and the perjury of every contemptible swearer. O God, spread out my hand in giving, freely and without stint, from spending in Your way; a hand that seeks Your mercy for those who hope in You, not inclining, in Your displeasure, toward hoarding, nor preferring, when Your good pleasure is within reach, riches over open-handedness. O God, when I have drawn down the treasures of Your abundant storehouses and prayed for the rain of Your gifts in mercy, do not turn my two hands away disappointed of the grant of Your bestowal; rather bind their rising to You to the descent of Your aid and the swiftness of Your answer, and hold them back from touching what the hands of those who tamper with Your sanctities and transgress Your command have long reached for. Let my eyes pour down, O God, with the flowing of tears and the streaming of weeping out of fear of You, and lower them from the moments You have forbidden them; make them humble before what may adorn them of the trinkets of this world and its flowers; and guard them, O God, from the drowsiness of slumber and the sweetness of sleep when the heedless lie down upon their beds. Bar my hearing, O God, from giving ear to what does not please You of the speech of the erring, and make it convey to my heart that which draws me near to You and earns Your good pleasure over me: the holding-lawful of Your lawful, the holding-forbidden of Your forbidden, good conduct at Your doors, and longing for the voluntary acts by which one hastens to Your good pleasure. Empty my heart, O God, of every breach in which I was heedless of Your command; take it back from what earns Your displeasure; and pour into it a full measure of Your love, that it may drive it to the nearness of intimate discourse with You and impel it to long for what is with You, of that which You have prepared for Your friends in the abode of Your honor. Question it about what has slipped away of the wreckage of this world, so weighty in the eyes of its people. Set my feet firm for You, O God, in the standing of devotion for Your intimate discourse, and in knocking at the door of Your answer, a door opened only to one who turns his face toward Your face; and aid me by them to recite Your Book at every hour of night and day, and grant them the strength of Your increase when I journey to You upon them through the pitch-dark of the far-off nights, that You may fulfill Your promise. Leave in me no limb but that I have made it ready for its task, no aim but that I have accomplished it, no rising resolve but that I have made it firm, no thread I mean to twist upon right guidance but that I have made it fast, and no craving of greed but that I have crushed it. O God, whatever failing has held me back from attaining a good benefit hoped for from none but You, and whatever visiting misfortune is lifted only by humble entreaty drawing near to You, bring me to it by Your bounty and Your generosity; for You do whatever You will and decree whatever You wish, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. So deal with me in all my states as befits You, by Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, the truthful, upon whom be greetings and peace all together, in well-being, O Lord of the Worlds.

He would say in his supplication, (ع): O Allah, You are more worthy of what befits You of Your pardon than I am of what befits me of Your punishment. O Allah, honor Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You are worthy of them and they are worthy of You. Do not discipline me with Your punishment, do not scheme against me with Your cunning, and do not lead me astray from where I do not know. O Allah, whoever is bettered by Your grace prospers, and whoever errs by his own sin perishes. No benefactor can dispense with Your support and Your aid, and no wrongdoer overcomes You, nor does any affair pass beyond Your power. So do with me what is worthy of You, for You are worthy of every good. Then he would pray for whatever he wished.

And it was among his supplications, (ع): O Lord, how many an enemy has drawn against me the sword of his aggression and honed for me the edge of his blade, sharpened the point of his resolve against me, and mixed for me his deadly poisons. His watchful eye never slept over me, and he resolved to visit me with harm and to make me drink its bitterness. Seeing my weakness before such heavy blows, and my helplessness to take revenge upon the one who set out to war against me, and seeing that I stood alone among the many who bore me enmity, You reinforced me with Your victory over him and strengthened me. You scattered his gathering after it had assembled, and raised my standing above his, and turned back upon him the arrows he had aimed at me. You choked him with his own rage and struck him with his own dart, so that he was thrown back upon himself after his arrogance, and humbled and brought low after his overbearing. Servile and captive he lay in the snare of his own rope, that very snare in which he had felt sure he would see me on the day of his triumph. To You be praise, as You are worthy of it, powerful and never overcome, forbearing and never hasty.

This is a supplication that Ali (ع) taught to al-Husayn (ع). He described to him such of its excellence that Allah, mighty and majestic, has made the reward binding upon whoever supplicates with it, a merit too long to recount. He took from him a covenant not to teach it to anyone save his family, his Shia, and his loyal ones, and al-Husayn (ع) pledged him upon that. He said to him: When you wish to ask Allah, mighty and majestic, for a need, or to call upon Him for any affair of this world or the hereafter, then say:

Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is the greatest, and there is no power nor strength except by Allah. Glory be to Allah in the depths of the night and at the ends of the day. Glory be to Allah in the morning and in the evening. Glory be to Allah when you enter upon evening and when you enter upon morning. To Him is praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon, and when you reach midday. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and He revives the earth after its death, and thus shall you be brought forth. Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they ascribe to Him. Peace be upon the messengers, and praise be to Allah, the Lord of the worlds. Glory be to the Owner of dominion and sovereignty. Glory be to the Owner of might, greatness, and compelling majesty. Glory be to the Living who does not die. Glory be to the King, the Most Holy. Glory be to the Everlasting, the Abiding. Glory be to the Living, the Self-Sustaining. Glory be to the High, the Most High. Exalted and sanctified is He, all-glorious and all-holy, our Lord and the Lord of the angels and the Spirit. Glory be to our Lord the Most High, exalted and sanctified is He.

O Allah, I have entered upon evening and upon morning within Your favor and Your well-being, so complete Your favor and Your well-being upon me, and grant me to render You Your thanks. O Allah, by Your light I was guided, by Your grace I seek help, and within Your favor I have entered evening and morning. O Allah, I call You to witness, and You suffice as a witness, and I call to witness Your angels, the bearers of Your throne, and all Your creation, that You are Allah, there is no god but You alone, having no partner, and that Muhammad is Your servant and Your messenger, may Allah bless him and his family. O Allah, record for me this testimony with You until I meet it on the Day of Resurrection, while You are pleased with me, for You are powerful over all things.

O Allah, to You be praise, a praise before which the sky lowers its shelter and by which the earth and all upon it glorify You. O Allah, to You be praise, a praise whose beginning ascends and whose end is never exhausted. O Allah, to You be praise, everlasting, abiding, without end. And to You be praise upon me, within me, and with me, and with my child, whether I sleep or wake, and when I have died and passed away and You alone remain, O my Master. O Allah, to You be praise with all the praises that are Yours, for all the blessings that are Yours. O Allah, to You be praise upon every vein at rest and every vein that throbs. To You be praise upon every morsel and every drink, every grasp of the hand, and upon every place where a hair grows. O Allah, to You be praise for Your forbearance after Your knowledge, and to You be praise for Your pardon after Your power. To You be praise, the Sender of praise. To You be praise, the Inheritor of praise. To You be praise, the Originator of praise. To You be praise, the Bestower of praise. To You be praise, the Ancient of praise, Raiser of ranks, Sender down of blessings from above the seven heavens, who brings out of the darknesses into the light, who changes evil deeds into good deeds and makes good deeds into ranks. O Allah, to You be praise, Forgiver of sin, Accepter of repentance, Severe in punishment, Lord of bounty, there is no god but He, to Him is the return. O Allah, to You be praise in the night when it covers over, and to You be praise in the day when it shines forth, and to You be praise in the hereafter and the first. O Allah, to You be praise to the number of the dust, the pebbles, the seeds, of mankind and jinn, of birds, beasts, and wild things. To You be praise to the number of what Your book has counted. To You be praise for all that Your knowledge has encompassed, a praise abundant, wholesome, and blessed.

Then he says: There is no god but Allah alone, having no partner. His is the dominion and His is the praise. He gives life and gives death, and He is Living and does not die. In His hand is all good, and He is powerful over all things, ten times.

Then he says: I seek forgiveness of Allah, other than whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Sustaining, for all my sins, and I repent to Him, ten times.

Then he says: O Allah, O Most Gracious, O Most Merciful, ten times. Then he says: O Compassionate, O Bestower, ten times. Then he says: O Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Owner of majesty and honor, ten times. Then he says: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, ten times. Then he says: Amin, Amin, ten times. Then ask your need, and pray upon the Prophet and upon his family.

Ali ibn al-Husayn (ع) would supplicate in the heart of the night, after every eye had grown still, saying in his supplication: My God, the stars of Your heavens have set, the eyes of Your creation have slept, and the voices of Your servants have fallen silent. The kings of Banu Umayyah have shut their doors upon themselves, set their guards to circle them, and veiled themselves from any who would ask them for a need or seek from them a benefit. But You, my God, are Living, Self-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep takes hold of You, and nothing occupies You away from anything else. The doors of Your heavens stand open to whoever calls upon You, and Your treasuries are not withheld from whoever asks of You, but are freely given. My God, You are the Generous who turns away no petitioner among the believers who asks of You, nor veils Yourself from any among them who seeks You. No, by Your might, their needs are not intercepted short of You, nor are they fulfilled by any other than You.

O Allah, You see me standing here, and You know my inmost secret. You look upon what is in my heart and upon what would set me right in my hereafter and my world. So come to me in this with Your bounty and Your generosity, my God. You see me awaiting death, and it is the appointed meeting and the standing before You. It has spoiled for me my food and my drink, choked my throat, driven sleep from my pillow and my rest, and kept me from repose. My God, how shall he sleep who fears the sudden coming of the angel of death in the watches of the night and the watches of the day? Rather, how shall the wise man sleep when the angel of death does not sleep in his vigil over him, seeking to seize his soul in the morning, in the depths of night, and in whatever hour it may be?

At these words he (ع) would weep, and would sob until his family and his loyal ones took fright at his weeping. They would come to him and find that he had pressed his cheek to the dust, saying: My Lord, I ask You for rest and repose at the hour of death, and for the passage to the abode of settled rest.

And among the supplications of Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع): O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and have mercy on my lowliness and my standing before You, my humble entreaty to You, my estrangement from people, and my intimacy with You. O my God, do not disgrace me, for You know me well, and do not chastise me, for You are able over me. O Allah, I seek refuge in You from abasement in life, from an evil sight at death, from an ill return in the grave, and from remorse on the Day of Resurrection. O Allah, I ask You for a life of contentment, a death of ease, and a return that is honorable, neither disgracing nor shaming. O Allah, Your forgiveness is wider than my sins, and Your mercy is more to be hoped for by me than my own deeds, so forgive me and have mercy on me. O Allah, to You be praise if I obey You, and Yours is the proof against me if I disobey You. No good deed of mine or of any other is ever lost with You, and there is no excuse for me or for any other in wrongdoing. O Allah, help me in my religion by my worldly life, and in my hereafter by my piety. O Allah, guard me in what I am absent from, and do not entrust me to myself in what I am present for. O You whom forgiveness does not diminish and whom sins do not harm, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, forgive me what does not harm You, and grant me what does not lessen You. O Allah, I ask You for ampleness in provision, for ease, forgiveness, mercy, health, piety, pardon, well-being, sufficiency, contentment, moderation, righteousness, gratitude, and success in all my affairs, for the hereafter and for this world, by the ease of all things and not by their hardship, O Generous One. My Lord, extend that same favor to my child, my family, my kin, and my brothers among the believing men and women and the Muslim men and women, the living of them and the dead, whom You have loved and drawn near, and to those whom I have begotten and those who begot me. O Allah, I ask You for patience in obeying You and patience away from disobeying You, for contentment with Your decree, for truthfulness in every place, for the realities of faith, and for gratitude for Your blessings that cannot be numbered. O Allah, bless, You and Your angels, Muhammad Your prophet and all the family of Muhammad.

An account of what is permissible and what is not permissible of speech and action within the prayer

It has been related to us from the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that speech, and the breaking of ablution, and turning away wholly from the Qiblah, and whatever is gross in action, all cut off the prayer. But supplication, glorification, the takbir, the recitation of the Quran, and whatever a servant addresses to his Lord within the prayer are not so. Though these be speech, they are not the speech that cuts off the prayer. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (ع) said, concerning that with which a man addresses Allah in prayer, that it is speech which does not cut off the prayer. They said: whoever is greeted with peace while he is in prayer, if he returns the greeting within himself or by a slight gesture, does not thereby cut off his prayer. They did not hold that a gesture, or a word said within oneself, is among the things that cut off the prayer. Yet to leave that aside and to turn wholly to the prayer is better. So if the one greeted leaves it until he has finished his prayer and returns the greeting after he has given the closing salaam, if he wishes, that is better.

They gave leave to one who sees a matter he must forbid, or fears something, or sees that he is about to miss something, to glorify Allah by saying "Glory be to Allah" while he prays, intending it as part of the Quran, since it is from it, or intending it as glorification, since that is permitted within the prayer. If the matter is one that carries no great harm, then to turn to his prayer and leave it aside is better. A gesture indicating what the worshipper intends is likewise in this same sense: if he points to one he wishes to address without turning his face from the Qiblah, there is no harm in it, though if he leaves it and turns to his prayer, that is better, if he finds in that some good.

They related that laughter in the prayer cuts it off, but that a smile does not cut it off, though it is disliked for the worshipper. They forbade blowing within the prayer, as when the worshipper blows upon the place of his prostration should he see upon it something he dislikes to prostrate over. If it is of what may not be prostrated upon, there is no harm in his removing it with his hand. If there is something in his place of prayer, let him move it aside, and if it is on the ground, let him move it beneath his feet, and if he takes it away with a garment, that is better. The worshipper should not spit toward his face nor to his right, but let him spit to his left, and let him not turn his face from the Qiblah. They forbade the cracking of the fingers in the prayer, which is that the worshipper bends them so that they crackle. This is of idle play and heedlessness in the prayer, and it cuts it off, since he who does it has no need of it. But if they crack from an act he did not intend, or from something he could not avoid, there is no harm in that.

They gave leave to scratch within the prayer for one to whom an itch comes, if he cannot bear it patiently and it distracts him from his prayer. They gave leave to the worshipper to kill a snake or scorpion he sees in the prayer, and every fearsome, harmful creature, and to kill a louse, a flea, or a gnat he finds upon his body or his garment while he is in prayer. They forbade deliberately toying with the hand upon the beard or elsewhere in the prayer, but gave leave for that if it happen without intent. They gave leave to recite from a written Quran in the prayer, and forbade stretching and yawning in the prayer. Whoever is overtaken by that without intending it does not thereby cut off his prayer. Likewise a sneeze does not cut off the prayer, though let the worshipper make it light if he is able, cover his mouth with his hand, praise Allah, and bless Muhammad and his family.

They forbade the worshipper to wipe his forehead of dust or of anything else he prostrates upon while he is in the prayer, but he may wipe that away when he has turned from the prayer, and let him not leave it. They forbade the tawarruk in the prayer, which is that the worshipper sets his hand upon his hip. And they forbade a man to pray with his face veiled, save from a necessity or an ailment.

As for the garments a person wears in prayer, the Messenger of God (ص) said: "Let every one of you fear God in his garment during his prayers." For this reason one should pray in the finest clothing he can find, for prayer is the best occasion on which a person adorns himself. We have narrated from the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that they permitted praying in a single garment, provided it covers the worshipper so that his awrah is not visible. If it is so light that it reveals him, they did not hold it sufficient for him to wear alone; he must have with it something that conceals the awrah. For a man, the awrah is what lies between the navel and the knees. For a woman, her whole body is awrah that she must cover in prayer, except her face. A free woman, if she wishes to pray, veils herself; a slave woman may pray without a veil, but she covers her head and does not leave her hair exposed. It is permissible for a man to pray in a wrapper that covers his awrah even if the rest of his body remains uncovered, when he finds nothing else. He should not do this deliberately while he has something else at hand; rather he wears what he finds. The worshipper drapes himself in a robe, a gown, or a cloak, laying its middle length across his shoulders, casting the end on his left over to his right and the end on his right over it to his left.

They forbade the wrapping known as ishtimal al-samma in prayer, which is that a man gathers the edge of the garment while it lies on his shoulder, draws it with his left hand to his hands, throws what was on his right over to his left, and winds himself in it as the people of the wilderness do, keeping his hands inside it. He should not pray wrapped in such a way. They permitted praying in the covering burnus, and they forbade sadl in prayer, saying it is the practice of the Jews. Sadl is to lay the robe from its middle length upon the shoulders and let its two sides hang loose beside the hands, without folding any of it back over the shoulders. They permitted a worshipper to pray girded with a sword, and they commended this for the Friday prayer, the two Eids, for Jihad and Ribat, and wherever a worshipper fears for himself in travel or otherwise. They saw no harm in praying in leather socks, and they permitted praying in sandals if they do not distract the worshipper and he can manage in them. They forbade praying in the garments of the polytheists that they had worn until such garments are purified. They commended that a woman pray wearing her ornaments if she has them, and that she not strip herself of this, even to the extent of tying about her neck a cord or some small thing by which she is distinguished from men; and they disliked that women divest themselves of ornament and of henna, or alter their palms, or resemble men in appearance. Everything permissible to wear is permissible to prostrate upon, whether of the growth of the earth or of other materials such as wool, hair, fur, and the like. The worshipper should stand firm in his prayer and not prostrate upon any foodstuff. They disliked that he prostrate upon any part of his own clothing, neither upon his sleeve nor upon the coil of his turban, and held that he must uncover his forehead so that it, or such part of it as he is able, reaches what he prostrates upon, together with his nose.

Concerning the Friday prayer, the Messenger of God (ص) said that four have what preceded them forgiven: the sick man when he recovers, the polytheist when he embraces Islam, the pilgrim when he completes his Hajj, and the one who returns from Jumuah in faith and in hope of reward. He said: "Pray abundantly upon me on Friday, for it is a day on which deeds are multiplied." And he said: "When Friday night comes, God Almighty sends down angels bearing pens of gold and silver and scrolls, and when the dawn breaks they record nothing but the prayers upon me and upon my Ahl al-Bayt until the sun sets. And angels stand at the doors of the mosques recording those who enter, each in his rank, first and then next, from the breaking of dawn until the Imam ascends the pulpit; when the Imam ascends the pulpit they fold their scrolls and enter to listen to the remembrance." He said: "There are three things which, if my nation knew the merit they hold, they would cast lots for them: the call to prayer, going early to Jumuah, and the first row in prayer." And he said: "Whoever goes early to the mosque on Friday and recites Surah Al Imran to its completion, seventy angels ascend with it and seventy angels receive it, and he is forgiven what lies between the two Fridays. And if he recites Surah al-Kahf, seventy angels ascend with it and seventy angels receive it, and he is gathered on the Day of Resurrection with a light spanning the distance between Mecca and Medina."

Ali (ع) said, concerning the words of God Almighty, "حَافِظُوا عَلَى الصَّلَوَاتِ وَالصَّلَوَاتِ الْوُسْطَى" ("Guard strictly the prayers and the middle prayer"), that the middle prayer is the Friday prayer, which on the remaining days is the noon prayer; and he used to command that the time of the sun's decline be carefully observed. He (ع) said: "Beware of forsaking attendance at the mosques, for one of you is soon to begin so that he comes to the mosque only on Friday, then falls back and comes one Friday and misses another, then falls back until he no longer comes at all, and so God sets a seal upon his heart." Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Hussein (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said: "Deeds are multiplied on Friday, so I love to increase my prayers and charity on that day." And Ali (ع) said: "Friday night is a resplendent night and its day is radiant. Whoever dies on Friday night, God writes for him a release from the torment of the grave; and whoever dies on Friday, God frees him from the Fire. Hell is kindled every day except Friday, for on it it is not kindled." And there is no harm in praying throughout the whole of Friday.

Ali (ع) said that the Friday prayer is an obligation, and gathering to it with the just Imam is an obligation; if a man forsakes it without excuse three times, he has forsaken three obligatory duties, and none forsakes three without excuse but a hypocrite. Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said that when Friday night comes, God commands an angel who calls out from the first of the night to its last, as He calls out every other night in the final third: "Is there one who asks, that I may give him? Is there one who repents, that I may turn to him? Is there one who seeks forgiveness, that I may forgive him? O seeker of good, draw near; O seeker of evil, hold back." And when the morning of Friday comes, God apportions the provisions among His servants until the sun rises. We have narrated from the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that they commended ghusl on Friday, and disliked taking medicine on Friday and Thursday lest it weaken the one who takes it from attending Jumuah; and they enjoined perfume and the finest clothing a person can find when he intends to go out to witness the Friday prayer. And the Messenger of God (ص) said that on Friday there is an hour in which no believing servant asks God for any good but that He grants it. Ali (ع), Abu Jafar, and Abu Abdullah (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said that it is from the sun's decline until an hour has passed.

They (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said that Jumuah is obligatory except upon the traveler, the woman, the child, the sick, and the owned slave, and whoever has an excuse; and whoever of these attends it, it suffices him in place of the noon prayer. They said that whoever is within two farsakhs of the congregational mosque, or less, is obliged to come to Jumuah; the farsakh is three miles, and the mile is three thousand cubits. If there are three miles between two congregational mosques, then Jumuah is obligatory in each of them, even within a single town. They said that the least by which Jumuah is established is five men, one of them the Imam; if they are fewer than five they do not gather for it but pray the noon prayer, for the Friday prayer with the Imam is equal to seventy prayers. This applies when they are in a settled town.

> فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةُ فَٱنتَشِرُوا۟ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱبْتَغُوا۟ مِن فَضْلِ ٱللَّهِ

Regarding the words of God Almighty, "يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَاةِ مِن يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ" ("O you who believe, when the call to prayer is made on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of God") [al-Jumuah: 9], they said this is a command of God, and the hastening is neither a trot nor a run; rather the merit lies in going early before the call. When the call to prayer is given, one may not stay behind, and the one walking to it walks, catching of it what he catches, without running or trotting. And regarding His saying, "فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ الصَّلَاةُ فَانتَشِرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَابْتَغُوا مِن فَضْلِ اللَّهِ" ("And when the prayer is concluded, disperse through the land and seek the bounty of God") [al-Jumuah: 10], this is a command of permission: as He commanded hastening at the call, He permitted departure after the prayer for whoever wishes. Whoever remains in the mosque, praying, listening to the remembrance, and sitting, has the merit and reward of that; and whoever leaves after the prayer is concluded, there is no blame upon him, for God has permitted it to him.

If one enters the mosque on Friday before the prayer, he prays voluntary prayers as he wishes before the Friday prayer, and he may pray voluntary prayers after it as he wishes. They disliked that one who comes when the people have already filled the mosque should climb over their necks. Ali (ع) said: "That I should sit out Jumuah is dearer to me than that I should hold back until, when the Imam has sat, I come stepping over the necks of the people." Whoever comes to the mosque when it is full should sit wherever he finds room, without stepping over the necks of the people; but if he finds them spread out so that he can walk between them to a space he sees at the front of the mosque, there is no harm in walking to it. They forbade speech once the Imam has ascended the pulpit, and enjoined the people to face him and to listen attentively to the sermon; when the Imam has finished, there is no harm in speech between that and the raising of the prayer.

When the Imam enters the mosque on Friday, he begins by ascending the pulpit, settles, turns his face to the people, greets them, and sits. The muezzins rise and give the call before him, and when they finish the adhan they sit. He rises, praises God and extols Him, prays upon the Prophet and his family, and exhorts the people as much as he is able and as is prepared for him; then he sits a brief sitting, rises, praises God again and extols Him, prays upon the Prophet and his family, and supplicates for the Imam and the believers as much as he is able. When he has finished, the muezzins rise and call the iqama; the Imam descends and leads the Friday prayer of two rakahs. In the first rakah, after the opening chapter of the Book, he recites Surah al-Jumuah, and in the second, after the opening chapter, Surah al-Munafiqun; he recites aloud, makes qunut after finishing the recitation in the second rakah, performs the tashahhud, gives the salam, and departs. He should deliver the sermon only while turbaned and girded with a sword, when that is possible and available to him. Whoever catches the last rakah of the Friday prayer with the Imam before the Imam raises his head from bowing has caught that rakah, and he adds a second rakah to it; but if he does not reach it until the Imam has raised his head, he has not caught Jumuah and prays four. If the people miss Jumuah they do not pray it; they pray the noon prayer, and if the Imam is absent and none is found to lead them in the congregational mosque, one of them leads them in the noon prayer of four rakahs.

> وَأَذَنٌۭ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦٓ إِلَى ٱلنَّاسِ يَوْمَ ٱلْحَجِّ ٱلْأَكْبَرِ

As for the prayers of the two Eids, God Almighty said: "شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ الَّذِي أُنزِلَ فِيهِ الْقُرْآنُ" ("The month of Ramadan in which the Quran was sent down"), through to His saying: "وَلِتُكْمِلُوا الْعِدَّةَ وَلِتُكَبِّرُوا اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَاكُمْ وَلَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ" ("that you may complete the number and magnify God for having guided you, and that you may give thanks") [al-Baqarah: 185]. And He said: "وَأَذَانٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ إِلَى النَّاسِ يَوْمَ الْحَجِّ الْأَكْبَرِ" ("And a proclamation from God and His Messenger to the people on the day of the Greater Pilgrimage") [al-Tawbah: 3]. We have narrated from the Imams of the household of the Messenger of God ﷺ that the day of the Greater Pilgrimage is the day of sacrifice, and that within it fall the Visitation, the Tawaf al-Ifadah, the slaughter, the shaving, the casting of the pebbles. They (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said that the takbeer is after the completion of the number of the fast, on the night of Fitr and the day of Fitr, and likewise the takbeer is made on Adha, and we shall mention that in its place, God willing.

Ali (ع) said: "It pleases me that a person free himself four nights in the year for prayer and the remembrance of God: the night of Fitr, the night of Adha, the night of the middle of Shaban, and the first night of Rajab." And Ali (ع) said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ص) address the people on the day of Adha, saying: This is the day of thajj and ajj. As for thajj, it is the blood you shed; whoever's intention is sincere, the first drop of it is an expiation for him of every sin. And as for ajj, it is supplication, so raise your voices to God. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, none departs from this standing place but is forgiven, save the one who persists in one of the major sins and does not resolve within himself to abandon it."

We have narrated from the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that they commended ghusl on the day of Fitr and the day of Adha before going out to the prayer ground; that one break his fast on the day of Fitr, with whatever is available, before going out to the prayer ground, and not eat on the day of sacrifice until he returns from the prayer; that the one going out to the two Eids wear the finest clothing he has and perfume himself with what perfume is at hand; and that the Imam be turbaned, whether in winter or summer. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (ع), when he wished to go out to the two Eids or to Jumuah, would say: "O God, whoever has prepared and made ready and equipped and provided himself to arrive before a creature, hoping for its bounty and its gift, then to You, O God, is my preparation, my making ready, my equipping, and my provisioning, hoping for Your bounty, Your gift, and Your favors. I have gone out to You, presenting no righteous deed I have advanced and no intercession of any creature in whom I have placed hope, save the intercession of Muhammad and his family. Rather I have gone out to You confessing my sins and my wrongdoing against myself. O Magnificent, O Magnificent, O Magnificent, forgive the great sin, for none forgives the great sin but You. O Exalted, O Magnificent, there is no god but You." And they (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) related the showing of weapons, equipment, and mounts on the day of Eid, that one may take pride in it and awe the enemy by it. The pulpit is brought out and set up on open ground; and if that is near the burial-ground, the cemetery, that is better. And the Imam goes out.

The Commander of the Believers (ع) used to go out to the two Eids in Kufa proclaiming the takbeer, and around him and before him a thousand of the city's elders and men of mature years proclaimed it with him. So too the people go out in their finest garments, with dignity, magnifying Allah, declaring His oneness, and praising Him as they go and as they return. When they reach the prayer ground, they sit without offering any voluntary prayer before the Eid prayer or after it. They sit in awe and reverence, remembering Allah, not pressing upon one another; each man sits where he has arrived. The rows are to be spaced so that every worshipper has room to prostrate and to bow, for whoever cannot manage that has no valid prayer.

When the imam arrives he begins with the prayer before the sermon, for such is the Sunnah of the Eid, and upon this was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those who came after him, until Uthman changed it. He had prayed with the people at an Eid, and when he finished the prayer most of them dispersed and did not stay to hear the sermon; so thereafter he set the prayer after the sermon, that they might not leave him as they leave on Friday. But it is not fitting that the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ be altered, or exchanged, or turned from that upon which he established it. Allah, mighty and exalted, has said: ﴿وَمَا آتَاكُمُ الرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ فَانتَهُوا﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. And He said: ﴿فَلْيَحْذَرِ الَّذِينَ يُخَالِفُونَ عَنْ أَمْرِهِ أَن تُصِيبَهُمْ فِتْنَةٌ أَوْ يُصِيبَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Nur: 63].

> لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا

The imam opens the prayer without adhan and without iqama, for there is neither adhan nor iqama for the two Eids. He pronounces the takbir al-ihram, then recites the Opening of the Book and Surah al-Shams wa duhaha, reciting aloud. Then he pronounces five takbeers, and between each two of them he offers a light qunut, which is to say: "O Allah, forgive me, have mercy upon me, grant me well-being, and pardon me in this world and the hereafter; You are powerful over all things." Then he pronounces the sixth takbir, rising with it, and prostrates two prostrations. He stands for the second rakah and recites the Opening of the Book and Surah Hal ataka hadith al-Ghashiyah. Then he pronounces four takbeers, and between each two of them a light qunut, then the fifth takbir, rising with it, and prostrates two prostrations. Then he gives the tashahhud and the salam.

He departs and ascends the pulpit, and the people fall silent, facing him, seated in their places, and he delivers two sermons as we described for the Friday prayer, save that in the sermon of Eid al-Fitr he mentions the Sunnah of the Fitr charity and enjoins it, and in the sermon of Eid al-Adha he mentions the Sunnah of the sacrifice and urges it upon whoever is able and possesses the means. Then he descends and departs, and the people depart. It is recommended that they return by a route other than the one on which they went out, if they find this possible and are able. Whoever misses the Eid prayer with the imam prays it alone in his house as four rakahs. Women are permitted to go out to the two Eids. Upon the people of the open country there is no obligation of gathering or of going out for the two Eids; the Eid is held only in the settled towns, wherever the Friday prayer is gathered. The Eid prayer is established by the same number that establishes the Friday prayer, five men one of whom is the imam; if they are fewer than that, no Eid is held for them. There is no Eid upon the traveler, though if the people of the wilderness attend, and any of the travelers choose to attend the Eid, that is good and there is merit in it for them. It is fitting that one of the people of the wilderness who is within two leagues of the town or nearer should witness the Eid.

If the day of Eid falls upon a Friday, they pray the Eid at its time and the Friday at its time, and the people of the wilderness return to their dwellings if these are distant, once the Eid prayer is done, which they prefer. If the people rise on the day of Eid not knowing of it, and then before midday it becomes clear to them that it is the Eid, they go out and pray the Eid and break their fast if it is Eid al-Fitr. But if they do not know of it until after midday, they break their fast and then go out the following day, at the hour of going out to the Eid prayer, and make up the Eid prayer just as they would have prayed it on the day itself. The time of going out to the two Eids is when the sun has risen somewhat, and they delay going out on the day of Fitr a little later than on the day of Adha.

The takbeer of the days of Tashreeq runs from the Fajr prayer on the day of Arafah to the Asr prayer on the last of the days of Tashreeq; after that Asr the takbeer is pronounced and then cut off. The takbeer of the days of Tashreeq is obligatory upon men and women, in travel and in residence, after every prescribed prayer, and there is no takbeer following a voluntary prayer. The takbeer of the days of Tashreeq is: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, wa lillahi al-hamd. Allahu akbar ala ma hadana, wa Allahu akbar ala ma razaqana min bahaim al-anam." So too is the takbeer while going out to the prayer ground on the day of sacrifice, and on the day of Fitr likewise, except that on it one does not say "for what He has provided us of the grazing beasts." The days of Tashreeq are the three days after the day of sacrifice, named so because in them the people spread the strips of meat, that is, they lay them out for the sun. The day of Arafah is the day before the sacrifice. The day of sacrifice is the day of Eid, following the day of Arafah. The day of settlement follows the day of sacrifice, named so because the people settle upon it at Mina. Then follows the first day of departure, then the last day of departure, which is the last of the days of Tashreeq; on it the takbeer is pronounced after the Asr prayer and then cut off. When the people pray in congregation during the days of Tashreeq, the imam gives the salam and pronounces the takbeer; when he has finished it, those behind him pronounce it, and he raises his voice and they raise theirs with the takbeer. Whoever the imam has preceded in part of the prayer, once the imam has given the salam, rises and makes up what he missed, then pronounces the takbeer after he has given the salam.

As for forgetfulness in the prayer: it is related from the Imams of the House of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that they said: whoever forgets the takbir al-ihram, the opening takbeer, and prays, then learns that he did not pronounce it at the beginning of his prayer, repeats the prayer. Whoever doubts whether he has bowed a rakah of his prayer bows, then prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. Whoever doubts and does not know whether he has prayed one rakah or two: if it is established that he prayed one, he builds upon it and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness; and if that is not established, he begins the prayer afresh, making the rakah he is in the first of his prayer, then prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. If he doubts and does not know whether he has prayed two or three, he builds upon certainty, which is two, and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. If he doubts and does not know whether he has prayed three or four, he gives the salam and prays two rakahs seated and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness; for if he had already prayed four, the two are a voluntary prayer for him, and if he had prayed only three, the two rakahs from sitting stand in the place of one rakah. Thus it has come from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: the prayer of the seated, without excuse, is half the prayer of the standing. If he doubts and does not know whether he has prayed two or four, he gives the tashahhud and the salam, then rises and prays two rakahs, reciting in them the Opening of the Book, gives the tashahhud and the salam, and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness; for if he had prayed only two, his prayer is complete, and if he had prayed four, his last two rakahs are a voluntary prayer for him, though he should fix his heart upon them as being of the obligation.

Whoever forgets the bowing repeats the prayer. Whoever forgets a prostration, when he remembers, gives the tashahhud and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. Whoever forgets the tashahhud prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness and gives the tashahhud after them and the salam. If he departs and forgets to give the salam, having given the tashahhud, then the salam of the tashahhud suffices him, meaning his words "peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." Whoever forgets the recitation but has completed the bowing and the prostration owes no repetition; he prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. But if he leaves the recitation deliberately, he repeats the prayer. If he forgets to sit for the first tashahhud and rises for the third rakah without sitting, then remembers before he bows, he sits, and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness after he has finished the prayer. In all that we have mentioned, the two prostrations of forgetfulness come after the salam. If he remembers before rising and before speaking, he prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness, then gives a light tashahhud, gives the salam, and departs. If he has forgotten and given the salam after two rakahs, then realizes this before he has left his prayer, he completes the prayer, gives the tashahhud, and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. Likewise, if he has left the prayer and spoken, he need only bring what remained upon him and prostrate the two prostrations of forgetfulness.

So too did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ do. He forgot and gave the salam after two rakahs of a prayer he had shortened, and departed. Dhu al-Yadayn said to him: "Has the prayer been shortened, or have you forgotten, O Messenger of Allah?" He said, "How is that?" He said, "You departed after two rakahs." So he rose to the people and asked, "Is what Dhu al-Yadayn said true?" They said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." Then he prayed two rakahs and gave the salam, then prostrated the two prostrations of forgetfulness, then gave the salam and departed.

Whoever forgets and adds to his prayer: if he had given the tashahhud at the end of his prayer and then rose and added, his prayer is complete and what he added is a voluntary prayer, and he prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. If he had not sat for the tashahhud, and the addition was a bowing, he repeats the prayer; but if the addition was only a prostration, he completes the prayer and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. Whoever forgets and does not know whether he added to his prayer or fell short, his mind inclining to nothing in particular, gives the tashahhud and the salam, then prays two rakahs reciting in them the Opening of the Book, gives the tashahhud and the salam, and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. Whoever doubts about the bowing after he has prostrated proceeds with his prayer; likewise if he doubts about the prostration after he has risen, he proceeds and owes nothing until he is certain; and likewise if he doubts about anything of his prayer after he has left it, he owes nothing until he is certain. Whoever neglects his prayer and abandons it deliberately prays it when he remembers. Whoever is often afflicted with forgetfulness proceeds upon his certainty and builds upon it and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. Whoever imagines within his prayer that he has broken his ablution proceeds with the prayer unless he is certain of it. Whoever forgets behind the imam while following him owes nothing.

As for what cuts off the prayer: whoever is met by something he fears for himself, his property, or another, or by some sudden matter that does not permit him to complete his prayer while he is within it, there is no harm in his cutting it off, then beginning and resuming the prayer. The breaking of ablution within the prayer cuts off the prayer; so when the worshipper breaks his ablution he leaves, performs the ablution, and resumes the prayer. Whoever vomits or has a nosebleed in the prayer, and is able to rinse away the vomit and wash off the blood without turning his face from the qibla, does so and builds upon his prayer; but if he turns his face from the qibla, he begins the prayer afresh. Whoever speaks in the prayer has cut it off and owes its repetition. Whoever, while in the prayer, remembers that he is in a state of major impurity or otherwise without purity, cuts it off, purifies himself, and begins the prayer afresh; and if he remembers this after he has prayed, he purifies himself and repeats the prayer, and if he was an imam, all who prayed by his prayer repeat theirs. The worshipper does not cut off the prayer on account of something passing before him, but wards it off as much as he can. Ali (ع) said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed one day, and there passed before him a woman, then a donkey passed, then a dog passed, while we were watching. When he had finished he said, "I have seen what you have seen; nothing cuts off the prayer of the believer. But ward off what you are able to ward off."

As for one who has been preceded in part of the prayer: when a man arrives while the imam is leading the people, and enters into their prayer, he pronounces the takbeer of consecration. If he reaches the imam before he bows, or before he raises his head from the bowing, he bows with him and counts that rakah. If he does not reach him until he has raised his head from the bowing, he enters with him in his prayer and prostrates with his prostration but does not count that rakah; he counts what comes after it and takes that as the beginning of his prayer. If the imam has preceded him by a rakah, he prays the second with him; and when the imam sits for the first tashahhud, the latecomer does not sit fully settled but sits poised to rise, and does not give the tashahhud. When the imam rises for the third rakah, it is the latecomer's second. When the imam prostrates, he prostrates with him; and when the imam rises for the third, the latecomer returns briefly to the ground, gives a light tashahhud, then rises. When the imam sits, the latecomer sits as he sat at first, poised, and does not give the tashahhud; and when the imam gives the salam, the latecomer does not give it but rises and makes up a rakah, then sits settled, gives the tashahhud and the salam, and departs.

If the imam has preceded him by two rakahs, he takes the one he caught with him as the first of his prayer; and when the imam gives the salam, the latecomer does not give it but rises and brings two rakahs to complete his prayer, then gives the tashahhud and the salam and departs. The tashahhud he performs at the imam's final one is, for him, the first tashahhud. So too, if he catches only a single rakah of the prayer, he builds upon it and makes it for himself the first of his prayer, observing at the imam's sitting and rising the like of what we have described for one who has missed a rakah. If it is the Maghrib prayer and the imam has preceded him by a rakah, he enters with him in the second, likewise taking it as the first of his prayer, and sits when the imam sits for the first tashahhud, poised as we described, without giving the tashahhud. When the imam rises for the second rakah, the latecomer takes it as his own second; and when the imam sits for the last tashahhud, the latecomer sits with him and gives, for himself, the first tashahhud. When the imam gives the salam, the latecomer rises and prays one rakah, sits, gives the tashahhud and the salam, and departs. If he does not catch the rakah with him, he takes what he has as the first of his prayer, and when the imam sits to give the tashahhud he sits as we described, poised, without giving the tashahhud; and when the imam gives the salam, he rises and prays a rakah reciting in it the Opening of the Book and a surah, then sits for the first tashahhud, then rises and completes his prayer. And if the imam has preceded him by a rakah in the Fajr prayer, and the imam sits for the tashahhud, the latecomer sits with him as we described, poised, without giving the tashahhud; and when the imam gives the salam, the latecomer rises and prays a rakah, then sits, gives the tashahhud and the salam, and departs. If the latecomer forgets and gives the salam with the imam's salam, then remembers, he makes up what he missed and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness. This is the teaching of the Imams of the House of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

If the imam has preceded a latecomer by one rakah in the Fajr prayer, and the imam sits for the testimony, the latecomer sits as well in the manner already described, poised and ready, but does not recite the testimony himself. When the imam gives the salutation, the latecomer rises and prays a single rakah, then sits, recites the testimony, gives the salutation, and departs. Should the latecomer forget that the imam had already given the salutation and give it with him, then remember, he makes up what he missed and performs the two prostrations of omission. This is the teaching of the imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

As for the time at which boys are commanded to pray, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The pen is lifted from three: from the child until he reaches puberty, from the sleeper until he wakes, and from the insane until he recovers." In this there is proof that prayer does not fall upon boys as a binding obligation until they reach puberty. Yet it has come down from Ali and the imams of his lineage (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that they directed boys to be taken to prayer once they can understand it, and to fasting once they can bear it, before puberty, not as a strict duty but so that they may be trained in it, grow accustomed to it, and settle into it. Then, when they arrive at the age of puberty, they will already know it, will have been keeping it, and will not be plunged into it all at once in a way that breeds weariness, restlessness, and indifference. For when habits are laid down early, they become like a second nature.

It has likewise come from them (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that whoever takes up a good deed, whether prayer or fasting or any of the other gates of righteousness, and persists in it, should hold to it without cutting it off before a full year has passed over it. By this they intended to lead people to good by degrees and to make it light upon them. Had they said, "persist in it forever," the weight of it would have fallen heavy on those who heard. But when a man is told, "keep to this for a year," it is easier for him, and once he has kept to it a year it becomes for him a nature and a habit he cannot cut off, for he has grown familiar with it, found ease in it, and taken comfort in it, so that it is hardly possible for him to abandon it. In the same spirit they commanded that boys be taken to prayer and fasting before puberty. They said: children are to be commanded to pray at seven years of age, and disciplined for neglecting it at nine. They are to be separated in their beds at ten, and this separation at that age is a precaution, since their nearness to one another in sleep coincides with their nearness to puberty and the first stirring of desire, lest their closeness in bed lead to anything to be feared. This is the discipline of the friends of Allah toward His servants, whom Allah has entrusted to their care and whose affairs of religion and of the world He has committed to their keeping.

> فَسِيحُوا۟ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ أَرْبَعَةَ أَشْهُرٍۢ

As for the traveler's prayer, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, has bestowed on my nation a gift He has bestowed on no other nation before it," an act of honor from Allah, mighty and majestic. It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is this gift?" He said: "The breaking of the fast and the shortening of the prayers in travel. Whoever does not do so has returned to Allah His gift." Ali (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ) said: "Whoever shortens the prayer in travel has accepted the relief of Allah, mighty and majestic, and his prayer is complete." And it was said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade that the prayer be prayed in full during travel. Jafar ibn Muhammad (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ) said: "I am innocent of anyone who prays four rakahs in travel." Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ) said that whoever prays the prayer in full while traveling, knowing that the sunnah is to shorten it, must repeat the prayer, but whoever does not know this need not repeat it.

They (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said that shortening in travel means to pray every prayer as two rakahs, except Maghrib, which is not shortened in travel or at home. They said that the traveler prays the sunnah and the supererogatory prayers as well; if he is journeying by day and the road presses him on, he prays the obligatory prayer as two rakahs and delays the last of the sunnah until he alights at night, when he makes it up together with the night prayer. This they held praiseworthy and did not approve its neglect. The traveler does not pray in full, nor does he pray fewer than the full number in the case of any obligatory prayer, whether in travel or at home.

They (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said that the distance of travel at which shortening and breaking the fast become obligatory is two barids, twenty-four thousand paces. The barid is four farsakhs, the farsakh is three miles, and the mile is three thousand cubits, which comes to one thousand moderate paces measured by a single leg, from where the right foot is lifted to where it is set down. Even if the place a traveler intends is but a single barid away, and he has there neither family nor dwelling, and intends to return from it within less than ten days, he shortens and breaks his fast until he departs. The traveler breaks his fast and shortens his prayers from the moment he leaves his house and sets out on his journey, until he returns and enters his house, provided he is pressing on in his travel.

If a traveler enters a congregational prayer led by residents, he gives the salutation after two rakahs and departs. If a traveler leads residents in prayer, he ends at two rakahs and then bids them complete the prayer. Both of these are disliked, as has been mentioned, because the ruling of the traveler in prayer is not the ruling of the resident. Whoever has an unpaid prayer from his time of residence and remembers it while traveling makes it up in full as it was owed. Whoever has an unpaid prayer from his travel and remembers it while resident makes it up according to how it was, shortened.

The traveler may pray voluntary prayers while mounted, wherever he turns, toward the Qibla or away from it. This rests upon the word of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿فَأَيْنَمَا تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ اللَّهِ﴾ "Wherever you turn, there is the face of Allah" [al-Baqarah: 115]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray voluntary prayers upon his mount on his return from the Farewell Pilgrimage, with the House behind his back. But this is permitted only in the supererogatory prayer; the obligatory prayer is not prayed except upon the ground, turned toward the Qibla. They forbade praying upon the beaten track, that is, the highway where people pass, or in the space between two roads.

At sea the traveler shortens the prayer and prays aboard the ship. If the ship turns, he turns his face with it toward the Qibla; if he cannot pray standing, he prays seated. One who is drowning, one who is naked, and one wading through water pray by gesture, making the prostration lower than the bowing, and the naked person likewise prays seated when he finds nothing to cover his nakedness.

Shortening is not for one who goes out merely to take his ease, nor for a governor making his rounds among his people, nor for a tax-gatherer moving about in his collection, nor for the hired driver, nor for those seafarers whose very calling is perpetual travel, nor for one who alights in his travel upon a household of his own intending to stay with them. Whoever alights at a place in his travel intending to remain ten days prays in full; if he intends less, he shortens. If his stay is drawn out without such intention, while he intends each day to depart, he shortens for as long as a month, and after the month he prays in full until he leaves.

As for the prayer of the sick, we have it from the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that if the sick person cannot pray standing, he prays lying on his back with the Qibla before his face in the direction of his feet, or lying on his right side with his face toward the Qibla, gesturing so that his prostration is lower than his bowing. Likewise, one who prays seated and cannot bow and prostrate does the same. One afflicted with a nosebleed that will not stop, or a wound that keeps discharging and cannot be bound and cannot be held back, performs ablution and prays in that state, for Allah is most ready to excuse His servant when He has tried him.

If the sick person cannot pray anything beyond the obligatory, then when he recovers he may, if he wishes, make up the sunnah and supererogatory prayers he left, and in that there is merit and reward, though their making-up is not binding as the making-up of the obligatory is binding. If he can pray seated with his legs folded, he folds them as he would fold them in sitting during the standing; if he cannot, he prays however he is able and it suffices him. It suffices him to recite the Opening of the Book alone, and if he can do no other, to say a single glorification in his bowing and his prostration when he can manage no more. If he is able to prostrate, he prostrates; if not, he nods with his head, making the prostration lower than the bowing; and if he cannot nod his head, he signals with what he can, his head or his eye, as he is able, for Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. If he is able to pray standing, he prays only so, unless standing strengthens his illness and increases it, in which case he may pray in the manner described according to what he can do. Whoever falls into a swoon makes up the prayers he missed, be they few or many, when he comes to.

As for the prayer of fear, Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿فَلَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُنَاحٌ أَن تَقْصُرُوا مِنَ الصَّلَاةِ إِنْ خِفْتُمْ أَن يَفْتِنَكُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إِنَّ الْكَافِرِينَ كَانُوا لَكُمْ عَدُوًّا مُّبِينًا وَإِذَا كُنتَ فِيهِمْ فَأَقَمْتَ لَهُمُ الصَّلَاةَ فَلْتَقُمْ طَائِفَةٌ مِّنْهُم مَّعَكَ﴾ "There is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are to you a clear enemy. And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a party of them stand with you" [al-Nisa: 101 to 102], down to His words: "a humiliating punishment." Thus Allah, mighty and majestic, granted the relief of shortening the prayer in the state of fear, making no exception in it of travel from residence. Abu Abd-Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad ibn Ali (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ) was asked about the prayer of fear and the prayer of travel, whether both are shortened, and he said: "Yes, and the prayer of fear is more deserving of shortening than the prayer of travel, for in the prayer of travel there is no fear."

We have it from the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed the prayer of fear in the campaign of Dhat al-Riqa. He divided his companions into two parties, stationing one facing the enemy and placing the other behind him. He said the opening takbir and they said it, he recited and they listened, he bowed and they bowed, he prostrated and they prostrated. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood, and this party prayed a further rakah on their own, gave the salutation one to another, and withdrew to their companions, standing in their place facing the enemy. Then the other party came and stood behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said the takbir and they said it, he recited and they listened, he bowed and they bowed, he prostrated and they prostrated, and he sat and they sat and bore witness. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave the salutation, they rose and made up a further rakah for themselves, bore witness, gave the salutation one to another, and withdrew.

They (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said: thus is the prayer of fear prayed, whenever it is possible, in all the prayers save Maghrib, which is not shortened, as was mentioned before. The first party prays one rakah with the imam and prays two rakahs for itself, according to what we have described of the prayer of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the other party prays two rakahs with him, so that each party may hear the recitation in the first two rakahs, in which he recites aloud.

They (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said: if they cannot pray in this manner and the fear grows severe, they pray mounted upon their beasts or standing on their feet, nodding with their heads and making the prostration lower than the bowing, neither dismounting nor prostrating upon the ground when they are unable to do so. If they cannot face the Qibla, they face it at the first takbir and then turn to meet the enemy. This is the word of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿فَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ فَرِجَالًا أَوْ رُكْبَانًا﴾ "If you are in fear, then on foot or riding" [al-Baqarah: 239]. If the fighting closes in and there is the clash of swords and the thrust of spears so that they cannot even gesture, they pray with the takbir alone, saying a takbir for each rakah with the intention of prayer. In just this way the Commander of the Believers, Ali (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ), and his companions prayed on the night and the day of al-Harir.

As for the eclipse prayer, Ali (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ) said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The moon was eclipsed while Jibril (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ) was with me, and I said to him: What is this, O Jibril? He said: Truly it is more obedient to Allah than you, and it has not disobeyed Allah since He created it; but this is a sign and a lesson. I said: What is to be done at such a time? He said: Prayer and the recitation of the Quran." When the sun or the moon was eclipsed, he (ع) would say to the people: "Hasten to your mosques."

We have it from the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that the prayer for the eclipse of the sun and of the moon is one and the same, save that the prayer for the eclipse of the sun is a little longer. When an eclipse occurs, the people are to be summoned to prayer without the adhan, and they gather at the Grand Mosque if they are in a city. The imam comes forward and they draw up behind him. He says the takbir aloud and they say it, then he begins the recitation with the Opening of the Book and the longest surah he is able to recite, reciting aloud. Then he says the takbir and bows, and they bow, and he remains long in the bowing and they remain with him for as long as he recited, glorifying and saying what is said in the bowing. Then he raises his head with a takbir and they raise theirs, and he recites the Opening of the Book and a long surah like the first, and after the recitation and before the bowing he makes the qunut, then bows in the same way and rises with a takbir. So he does through five bowings, making the qunut after each pair. When he raises his head from the fifth, he says: "Allah hears the one who praises Him," saying this only there and in the tenth, at which he prostrates. In the remaining bowings he says "Allahu akbar" when he raises his head, and then prostrates.

He draws out the prostration as he drew out the bowing, glorifying and saying what is said in prostration. Then he raises his head and sits a while between the two prostrations, saying what is said between them in its fullest form, then makes the second prostration in the same way, rises, and prays a further five bowings like the first. Then he prostrates and sits for a long testimony in which he calls upon Allah, turns to Him in longing, and asks Him for what he can of this world and the Hereafter in supplication, and then gives the salutation. If the eclipse has cleared, he departs; if not, he remains seated in his place facing the Qibla and bids the people sit likewise, reciting the Quran, supplicating, and remembering Allah until it clears or passes away.

The eclipse prayer is not prayed until the eclipse is seen and made plain.
