From Muzdalifah the Messenger of Allah (ص) came down toward Mina, and when he reached Muhassir, the valley that lies between Muzdalifah and Mina, he quickened his pace a little and took the middle road that brings the pilgrim out at the Great Jamrah. He went on until he reached the jamrah beside the tree and pelted it with seven pebbles. Then he came to Mina, offered his sacrifice, and shaved his head. Hastening through Muhassir is a Sunnah, and one should hasten through it as the Messenger of Allah (ص) did. On that day the Jamrat al-Aqabah is thrown before the sacrifice; then one slaughters and shaves, and there is no harm in whichever of these he begins with.

Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said: the pebbles for the jamarat may be taken from Muzdalifah or from other places lying toward Mina. Whoever is at Mina should not carry pebbles from one jamrah to another; rather, the pebbles for all the jamarat are taken from a single place. It is recommended that they be gathered up one by one, dark and speckled, about the size of a fingertip, and it is disliked to break them off from larger stones. It is recommended to perform the ritual washing before throwing them. The one who throws should keep Mina on his right and the House on his left when he means to throw, and should throw from the floor of the valley, not from above it. Abu Jafar ibn Ali (ع) said: when you throw the jamarat, pronounce the takbir with each pebble you cast.

Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said: whoever throws the Jamrat al-Aqabah on the Day of Sacrifice before slaughtering, then comes to Mina and slaughters and shaves, then proceeds to the House and circumambulates it seven times and performs the say between al-Safa and al-Marwah seven times as well, and this is the circumambulation of the Hajj, then returns and performs the circumambulation of the women, when he has done all of this, everything becomes lawful to him that ihram had forbidden to the muhrim by reason of his consecration. He then returns to Mina and remains there through the days of Tashriq, throwing the jamarat each day after the sun has passed its zenith. Each jamrah is pelted with seven pebbles, beginning with the lesser, then the middle, then the greater. He has latitude to throw at any hour of the day, though it is preferable that he be in a state of purity. The Messenger of Allah (ص) used to walk to the jamarat when he threw them.

Ali (ع) threw the jamarat both on foot and mounted, and there is no fixed prescription in this. The Messenger of Allah (ص) granted the herdsmen a dispensation to throw the jamarat by night, and whoever misses throwing them by day may throw them by night. Whoever places the pebbles of one jamrah upon another should repeat the throwing, beginning with the lesser jamrah and ending with the greater, which is the Jamrat al-Aqabah. The jamarat are thrown on behalf of the sick, and whoever misses any part of the throwing makes it up when he remembers, or appoints someone to make it up for him. Whoever hastens his departure within two days leaves the pebbles that remain with him and does not throw them at the jamarat after he has departed.

> وَلَا تَحْلِقُوا۟ رُءُوسَكُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ ٱلْهَدْىُ مَحِلَّهُۥ

As for the sacrificial offering, Allah Almighty said: "They are the ones who disbelieved and turned you away from the Sacred Mosque, and the sacrificial offerings from reaching their place of slaughter" [al-Fath: 25]. And He, Blessed and Exalted, said: "Do not shave your heads until the sacrificial offering reaches its place of slaughter" [al-Baqarah: 196]. The place of slaughter for the offering brought in a single Hajj, or in a Hajj joined to an Umrah, is Mina; the place of slaughter for the offering brought in a single Umrah is Mecca; and each is slaughtered in its own place. When the Messenger of Allah (ص) brought forward his offering he slaughtered it at the place of slaughter in Mina and said: "This is the place of sacrifice, and all of Mina is a place of sacrifice." So the people slaughtered at their own encampments. It is preferable that a man attend to the slaughter of his offering and his sacrificial animal himself, or slaughter it with his own hand; and if he is unable, let his hand be together with the hand of the one who slaughters; and if he is unable even for that, let him stand over it while the butcher acts in his stead. He should entrust this only to a Muslim.

The Messenger of Allah (ص) made Ali (ع) a partner in his offering. All the offerings that the Messenger of Allah (ص) brought, and those that Ali (ع) brought from Yemen, amounted to one hundred camels. The Messenger of Allah (ص) slaughtered sixty-three of them with his own hand, bound and standing, drawing near to him one after another, and he commanded Ali (ع), who slaughtered the rest. Then he ordered that a portion from each be placed in a pot and cooked; and the Messenger of Allah (ص) and Ali (ع) ate of that flesh and sipped of its broth, so that they might partake of every one of them, for Allah has said: "when their flanks fall, eat of them."

When Ali (ع) slaughtered his offering or sacrificed his devoted animal, he would say: "I have turned my face toward the One who created the heavens and the earth, as a sincere Muslim, and I am not among the polytheists. Truly my prayer, my devotion, my life, and my death are for Allah, the Lord of the worlds; no partner has He. Thus have I been commanded, and I am among the Muslims. O Allah, this is from You and to You. In the name of Allah." Then he took the knife to it. The naming of Allah suffices for that, and its omission is not permitted except for one who forgets; when he remembers, he names Allah. Whoever cannot find an offering to bring on his own should share with others in whatever he is able and can manage, and the more he does of this, the better.

The best of offerings is the she-camel, then the male camel, then the female of the cattle, for it was narrated from Ali (ع) that the female of the cattle is preferable to the male; and the name "badanah" applies to both camels and cattle. Then come the males of the cattle, then the ram of the sheep, which is better than the muja, which is the one whose testicles have been bound or crushed; and the muja is better than the mustalim, which is the one whose testicles have been cut away; and this is better than the ewe; and the ewe is better than the ram of the goats; and the ram of the goats is better than the female of the goats. None of all these suffices except the mature animal or the thani, save the sheep, of which the yearling suffices. Best of these is the mulh, whose whiteness is mingled with black in places, so that its muzzle is black, as are the sockets about its eyes, the extremities of its fore and hind legs, and the tip of its tail; and it was said that this is the description of the ram that was sent down to Ibrahim (ع).

Among offerings and sacrificial animals the plump is preferred, and the lean is disliked unless a man did not intend it, having bought it fat only for it to grow thin in his keeping. They forbade the animal whose horn is wholly broken; and if only the outer part is broken, it is called aqsam. They directed that the eye and the ear be inspected carefully, meaning (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that one look to this so that there be no defect. They forbade the animal whose udder teats, that is, the nipples of the udder, have been severed; and likewise the mangy, the aged, and the one whose ear has been cut off; and they disapproved of the muqabalah, whose ear has been cut at the front, and the mudabarah, whose ear has been cut at the back, and the sharqa, whose ear has been split in two, and the kharqa, in whose ear there is a round hole. As for a defect that befalls the animal after a man has bought it and dedicated it as an offering, nothing is required of him, and it suffices him. Its dedication is effected by marking it or garlanding it.

The marking of camels and cattle is that they be pierced in the hump on the right side with a piece of iron until their blood flows over it, so that the animal may be known as an offering should it stray. The ox is garlanded, and the sheep too when it is offered. The camel is draped with a covering cloth, which is given in charity when it is slaughtered. If the camel is disabled before it reaches its destination, it is slaughtered, a sandal is dipped in its blood and it is garlanded with it, and it is left so that whoever passes by of those for whom eating the offering is lawful may know that it is an offering and cut from it and eat, if he wishes. Of these offerings, what is voluntary its owner may eat from and feed to whomever he wishes; but what is obligatory, which is that due for a vow, or as recompense for game hunted, or for spoiling some part of the Hajj, of that he eats nothing. And the offering may not be sold, whether it is obligatory or otherwise.

Whoever's offering is disabled before it reaches its destination and who then finds no replacement bears nothing further; and if it strays, he buys another in a different place. If the offering he buys is the obligatory one, that is, if he has marked or garlanded it, he slaughters both together; if he has not dedicated it, then he has a choice in the matter. If a man's offering is misled together with the one who bought it, its owner may take it if he wishes, and it suffices for him but does not suffice for the one who slaughtered it; and he may claim its price, if he wishes, from the one who sold it to him. Whoever finds a stray offering should announce it, and if he finds no one who seeks it, he slaughters it on the last of the days of Tashriq on behalf of its owner. Whoever has his offering slaughtered and then has part of it stolen, it suffices for him. They (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) made obligatory the presentation of the offering, which is that a man take it from Mina to Arafah and stand with it there, and at Muzdalifah, and at all the ritual stations, and then slaughter it. Whoever slaughters a voluntary offering may eat of it, give charity from it, and feed of it whatever he wishes; and there is no fixed time for this.

Abu Abd Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) was asked about the words of Allah Almighty, "So eat of it and feed the poor and the wretched," and His saying, "eat of it and feed the contented and the beggar who importunes." He said: the poor man is the one who does not beg of people, and the wretched is in a harsher state than he and more sorely pressed. The contented is the one who is satisfied with what is given to him, who does not grow angry, nor cry out, nor twist his mouth in vexation. The beggar who importunes is the one who passes by presenting himself. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (ع) used to test the people in this so that the contented might be known from others: when a beggar came to a stop before him, he ordered that the head of the sacrificial animal be given to him. If he took it and passed on rejoicing, not vexed, he ordered that he be given of the meat as well; but if he was vexed and left it and went his way, he knew that he was not of the contented.

They disliked (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that anything of the offerings be taken out of Mina, except a small thing to make use of, such as some of the hump for medicine, or something of the hide, the wool, the fur, the sinew, or the hair, for such as one has need of on a journey. They favored that the hides of the offerings and sacrificial animals be given in charity, though they permitted their use, and that the butcher be given some of them and of the covering cloth. They forbade the offering of the jallalah, which is the animal that feeds upon dung and filth, and the eating of its flesh, until it has been cleansed by fodder and confined for a known period; and likewise its milk is not to be drawn until it has been cleared: the she-camel and the camel forty days, cattle twenty days, sheep seven days, ducks five days, and chickens three days. They forbade riding the offering in a way that would harm or weaken it, and loading burdens upon it, and putting it to work in the same manner; but there is no harm in what neither weakens it nor injures it. Whoever forgets to slaughter at Mina slaughters at Mecca when he remembers. The days of Mina are three following the Day of Sacrifice. The day after the Day of Sacrifice is the first of them, and it is called the Day of Qarr, because one settles at Mina upon it and does not depart, nor leave Mina upon it except to visit the House and circumambulate. The second is the Day of the First Departure, as Allah Almighty said: "Whoever hastens within two days, there is no sin upon him," meaning the hastening of the departure from Mina. The third is the last of the two days of departure.

As for the shaving and the shortening, Allah Almighty said: "Allah has fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you shall surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety, with heads shaved and hair shortened" [al-Fath: 27]. Shaving is what is done with the razor, and shortening is what is taken with scissors from the ends of the hair, leaving some of it. It has been narrated from the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that shaving is better than shortening, and that the Messenger of Allah (ص) shaved in the Farewell Pilgrimage, and some of the people shaved and some of them shortened. The Messenger of Allah (ص) said, "O Allah, have mercy upon those who shave." One who heard him said, "And those who shorten, O Messenger of Allah?" He said, "O Allah, have mercy upon those who shave and those who shorten." They ordered (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that with the shaving one take also from the sides of the beard and the mustache and pare the nails, and that the razor reach to the two prominent bones beneath the temples level with the ears. We have mentioned that the bald man and the one whose head is close-shorn each passes the razor over his head. The woman, when she comes out of ihram, cuts something from the ends of her hair and does not shave her head or any part of it.

Whoever forgets to shave, or does not know of it, until he has departed from Mina should shave wherever he recalls or learns of it; and if he is near to Mina he returns to it and shaves there; and if he shaves after he has drawn far from it, he sends his hair to Mina and has it cast there, if he is able. They ordered (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that whatever falls of the hair be buried. It has been narrated from Ali (ع) that he said, "Bury this hair, for everything that falls from the son of Adam while he is alive is dead matter that must be buried." Ali ibn al-Husayn (ع) used to bury his hair in a hollow at Mina when he shaved, saying at that time, "O Allah, grant me for every hair a light on the Day of Resurrection."

> ثُمَّ لْيَقْضُوا۟ تَفَثَهُمْ وَلْيُوفُوا۟ نُذُورَهُمْ وَلْيَطَّوَّفُوا۟ بِٱلْبَيْتِ ٱلْعَتِيقِ

As for what the pilgrim does at Mina, Allah Almighty said: "Then let them complete their rites and fulfill their vows and circumambulate the Ancient House" [al-Hajj: 29]. It has been narrated from Ali (ع) that he said: the completing of the rites is the throwing, the shaving, the vows, the walking, and the sacrifices; and the circumambulation of the Ancient House is the Circumambulation of the Visit, which is the Circumambulation of the Overflowing, the Circumambulation of the Hajj, of which I have already spoken in the chapter on Circumambulation. It falls on the Day of Sacrifice: the people visit the House after they have shaved and slaughtered at Mina, then return to the House and circumambulate it, then return to Mina, having become free of everything from which their consecration had bound them, as I have mentioned; and it matters not with which he begins, whether with shaving or with slaughtering. It is recommended thereafter to hasten the Circumambulation of the Overflowing on the Day of Sacrifice for the one performing tamattu, while they permitted the qarin and the one performing Hajj alone to delay it. There is no harm in throwing the jamarat before shaving and slaughtering, or after them; but one does not make the visit before he has shaved, slaughtered, and thrown, unless he does so forgetfully or in ignorance, in which case nothing is required of him, and he shaves, slaughters, and throws when he turns back. And he does not spend the nights of Mina away from Mina; whoever spends a night away from it deliberately owes a blood offering for each night he spends away, and whoever does so in ignorance or forgetfulness owes nothing, and Allah forgives them.

It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ص) shortened his prayer in Mina and commanded that Allah the Almighty be remembered abundantly during the days spent there. Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) commented on the words of Allah the Almighty, ﴿فَإِذَا قَضَيْتُم مَّنَاسِكَكُمْ فَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ كَذِكْرِكُمْ آبَاءَكُمْ أَوْ أَشَدَّ ذِكْرًا﴾ "When you have fulfilled your rituals, remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance" [Al-Baqarah: 200]. He said that when the polytheists would settle in Mina, they would boast of their fathers and recount the glories of their ancestors, and so Allah the Almighty commanded the Muslims to put in the place of that the remembrance of the Almighty.

They held it disapproved (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) to fast on the day of the sacrifice and the days of Tashreeq. They said that when the pilgrim throws the Jamarat al-Aqaba al-Kubra on the day of sacrifice, he is released from everything that was forbidden to him in the state of ihram, except hunting, women, dwelling outside of Mina, and perfume. When he then performs the circumambulation of the House and the say between al-Safa and al-Marwah, everything that was forbidden to him in ihram becomes permissible, except women; and once he performs the Tawaf al-Nisa, everything becomes permissible to him. They said that the takbir during the days of Mina is to be said after every obligatory prayer, the worshipper saying it after the taslim and before he rises: "Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, la ilaha ill-Allah, wa Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar wa lillahi al-hamd. Allahu Akbar for what He has guided us to, and Allahu Akbar for what He has provided us of the grazing livestock." He may visit the House each day of Mina if he wishes and perform voluntary circumambulation as much as he wishes during the day, then return and spend the night in Mina.

Concerning the departure from Mina, Allah the Almighty said, ﴿وَاذْكُرُواْ اللَّهَ فِى أَيَّامٍ مَعْدُودَاتٍ فَمَن تَعَجَّلَ فِى يَوْمَيْنِ فَلاَ إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ وَمَن تَأَخَّرَ فَلا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ لِمَنِ اتَّقَى﴾ "And remember Allah during the appointed days. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for the one who fears Allah" [Al-Baqarah: 203]. Abu Abd Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said that this refers to the stay in Mina: if you wish to remain, you have done well, and if you wish to hasten your departure in two days, you may do so, as Allah the Almighty has said. Whoever hastens his departure on the second day of Tashreeq, which is the third day after the day of sacrifice, should not depart until he has prayed the noon prayer and thrown the jamarat; thereafter he may depart if he wishes, between then and sunset. If the sun sets upon him, he stays the night, and then belongs to the people of the third day and may depart whenever he wishes, from the beginning of the day to its end, after he has prayed Fajr and thrown the jamarat. It is mentioned that one should send his baggage ahead toward Makkah before the departure. It is recommended for whoever departs from Mina to descend at al-Muhassab, which is al-Bat-ha, and to tarry there a little before continuing on. So the Messenger of Allah (ص) did: when he came to al-Muhassab he descended, remained for an hour, and then set out again.

It was said that whoever is among the first to depart may remain in Makkah until the people have shaved. When the people move on to Makkah, whoever desires to enter the House should enter it if he is able, and whoever does not enter owes nothing. Abu Abd Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said: If you are able to enter the House, enter it whenever you wish; but if you fear the crowd, do not endanger yourself. And he mentioned the account of a people who perished in the crush within it.

He said that it is recommended for whoever wishes to enter the Kaaba to perform a ritual bath. Upon entering, after praising Allah as He deserves and sending prayers upon the Prophet and his family, one says: "O Allah, You have said, and whoever enters it is safe, so make me safe from Your punishment, and cleanse my heart of arrogance, hypocrisy, ostentation, and doubt regarding Your religion, and secure me from my fear of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. O Allah, whoever has arrayed himself, or equipped himself, or made ready, or prepared for a journey to some created being in hope of his gift and his bounty, to You, my Master, has been my arraying, my equipping, and my preparation, in hope of Your gift and Your bounty. So do not disappoint my hope today, and do not turn me away today in disappointment from Your House. You have made it sacred, and You are the most generous of those whose house is visited. O Most Great, there is no god but You."

He said that whoever wishes to pray voluntarily inside the House should do so, and it is recommended to pray between the two pillars, upon the red marble, for there is no spot on earth better than it, and upon it the Messenger of Allah (ص) prayed. He then rose and faced the back of the House in his prayer, then stood and faced each corner of the House, supplicating at it, before returning to the red marble to pray upon it. He said that one does not pray an obligatory prayer inside the Kaaba, nor is it permissible to pray upon its roof.

He said (ع) that whoever intends to depart from Makkah should make his final act with it a circumambulation of the House, performing seven rounds, then bidding it farewell and placing his hand between the Black Stone and the Door, saying: "O Allah, I am Your servant, and the son of Your servant, and the son of Your handmaid. You carried me upon Your mount and conveyed me through Your land until You brought me into Your sanctuary. O Allah, this is Your House, and I have come to it, and I have hoped, in the goodness of my thought of You, that You would forgive me my sins. So if You have forgiven me, then increase Your pleasure toward me and grant me nearness with You; and if You have not yet forgiven me, then from this hour forgive me, before I depart from Your House. This is the hour of my departure, if You have granted me leave, without turning away from You, nor from Your House, nor exchanging You or Your House for any other. So guard me on my right and on my left, behind me and before me, until You bring me to my family; and when You have brought me to them, do not forsake me, and take me unto Yourself upon that upon which You have taken Your righteous servants, for You are more worthy of that than Your creation and than I." Then he clings to the House and says: "O Allah, do not make this the last of my covenant with Your House." When he has gone out, he stands at the door of the mosque, turns his face toward the House, fills his eyes with the sight of it, raises his hands toward the sky, and says: "O Allah, send me back triumphant, prospering, shown mercy, and forgiven. O Allah, if You cause me to die, forgive me; and if You grant me life, provide me a Hajj in the coming year, and do not make this the last of my covenant with Your Sacred House."

He said (ع) that it is recommended for one who intends to leave Makkah to buy dates for dirhams, or whatever he is able, and to give them in charity, intending thereby to atone for whatever befell him during his ihram and his Hajj of neglect or shortcoming. And he said (ع) that one departing from Hajj should not hurry his travel as though he were turning away from what he dislikes toward what he loves; rather, let him depart with tranquility upon him. And Ali (ع) would not accept the testimony of one who races ahead of the pilgrims. One day he went out to al-Rahbah and saw a gathering. He asked what this was, and was told it was one who had raced ahead of the pilgrims. He said: "No welcome and no greeting. You have shortened the prayer and wearied the mount at noon."

As for the individual Umrah, Allah the Almighty said, ﴿وَأَتِمُّوا الْحَجَّ وَالْعُمْرَةَ لِلّهِ﴾ "And complete Hajj and Umrah for Allah" [Al-Baqarah: 196]. The Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), and those of the reciters who agreed with them, read Umrah in the accusative, giving it the meaning of an obligation: complete the Hajj and the Umrah. They said that it is obligatory. Some of those who differed from them read "and Umrah for Allah" in the nominative, as though they cut off the speech after His words "and complete the Hajj," and began anew, so that the obligation fell upon what was for Allah the Almighty. Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said that Umrah is an obligation in the same rank as Hajj, because Allah the Almighty says, "Complete the Hajj and the Umrah." It was narrated from Ali (ع) that he said Umrah is obligatory. And it was narrated from al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) that he said: Umrah to Umrah is an expiation for what lies between them. The Messenger of Allah (ص) said: An Umrah in the month of Ramadan equals a Hajj. For the individual Umrah, one who performs it alone enters ihram from the miqat, avoids what the one in ihram avoids, and forms the intention. When he comes to the House he circumambulates it seven times, performs the say between al-Safa and al-Marwah, prays the two rakahs of the circumambulation, and is released; this is the Umrah. If he has driven a sacrificial animal, he slaughters it at Makkah. Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said: Perform Umrah in whichever of the months you wish, and the most excellent of that is an Umrah in the month of Rajab. If you perform Umrah in the month of Hajj and then depart, it is an individual Umrah; but if you then perform Hajj in that same year, you are one performing Qiran.

> وَلَا تَحْلِقُوا۟ رُءُوسَكُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ ٱلْهَدْىُ مَحِلَّهُۥ

Concerning repulsion and siege, Allah the Almighty said, ﴿هُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَصَدُّوكُمْ عَنِ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ وَالْهَدْىَ مَعْكُوفًا أَن يَبْلُغَ مَحِلَّهُ﴾ "It is they who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and the offering, prevented from reaching its place" [Al-Fath: 25]. And He, Blessed and Exalted, said, ﴿فَإِنْ أُحْصِرْتُمْ فَمَا اسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ الْهَدْيِ﴾ "If you are prevented, then whatever offering is feasible" [Al-Baqarah: 196]. Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said that repulsion is prevention, and siege is illness. He said (ع) that the Messenger of Allah (ص) set out from Medina in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah with more than a thousand of his companions, intending Umrah. He entered ihram from Dhu al-Hulayfa, and they entered ihram, and he drove the sacrificial animals, collared them, and marked them. Word of this reached the Quraysh, and this was before the conquest of Makkah, and they gathered their forces against him and went out to bar his way. When he was near Asfan, their news came to him. He said: We have not come to fight anyone; we have come only as pilgrims of Umrah. If the Quraysh wish, I will make a truce with them for a term and leave the way open between me and the people; then, if they wish to enter into that which the people have entered, they may enter, and if they refuse, I will fight them until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges. The emissaries went back and forth between him and the Quraysh, and there was in that a long account, the end of which was that he (ص) made a truce with them for a term, on the terms that he would turn back that year and perform Umrah, if he wished, the following year, along with whoever wished to accompany him. He then slaughtered the sacrificial animals he had driven where he stood, and they cut their hair short, and he turned back, and the Muslims with him turned back.

This is the ruling of one who is turned back from the House, and what he must do when he has made the Hajj or the Umrah, or both together, binding upon himself, which is only when he has passed the miqat. As for one turned back before reaching the miqat, he simply turns away, whether he entered ihram or not; and if he had driven a sacrificial animal, he turns back if he wishes and does with it as he pleases, because he had not yet made it binding, since, as mentioned before, the offering is made binding by its marking and its collaring, and that is only after entering ihram from the miqat. Whoever enters ihram from short of the miqat is not in a valid ihram and has done wrong and departed from the Sunnah.

> وَلَا تَحْلِقُوا۟ رُءُوسَكُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ ٱلْهَدْىُ مَحِلَّهُۥ

As for siege, it is illness, as al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) explained in the words of Allah the Almighty. He (ع) was asked about a man beset by illness who had with him an offering he had sent ahead with his companions, appointing them a set time: if he is in Hajj, the place of slaughtering the offering is on the Day of Sacrifice; and if he is in Umrah, let him reckon the measure of his companions arrival in Makkah and the hour he has appointed for them, and when that hour comes, he cuts his hair short and is released. This, again, is only when he had entered ihram from the miqat and then fell ill afterward. But if he had not yet reached the miqat, he may turn back if he wishes or remain, because the obligation of Hajj had not yet become binding upon him. It was narrated that al-Husayn ibn Ali (ع) set out from Medina intending Umrah, and when he came to al-Suqya he fell ill, and news of him reached Ali (ع), who was in Medina. He came to him and said: My son, what do you complain of? He said: I complain of my head. So Ali (ع) called for a camel and slaughtered it on his behalf, shaved his head, and returned him to Medina; and when he recovered, he went out and performed Umrah. Likewise, whoever is besieged by illness after entering ihram for Hajj, or intending Umrah, or both together, is obliged to shed blood, as Allah the Almighty said, ﴿فَإِنْ أُحْصِرْتُمْ فَمَا اسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ الْهَدْيِ﴾ "If you are prevented, then whatever offering is feasible" [Al-Baqarah: 196], and that is a sheep or more; then he turns back. When he recovers from his ailment, he goes out and makes up what he was besieged from of Hajj, or Umrah, or both together.

The one besieged by illness does not approach women until he completes what he was besieged from, while the one merely turned back may approach women and is not obliged to make up what he was turned back from. This is entirely the word of the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ). Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) was asked about one who was besieged and then recovered, whether women became lawful for him. He said: No, not until he circumambulates the House. He was asked: Then why did women become lawful for the Messenger of Allah (ص) when he returned from al-Hudaybiyyah, though he had not circumambulated the House? He said: The two are not alike. For the one turned back, that is lawful; but for the one besieged, it is not.

Concerning Hajj on behalf of the incapacitated and the deceased, a woman from Khatham came to the Messenger of Allah (ص) and said: O Messenger of Allah, my father is an old man, grown too feeble to move, and the obligation of Hajj has come upon him. Shall I perform Hajj on his behalf? The Messenger of Allah (ص) said: Yes, do so, for were there a debt upon your father which you discharged, would that not suffice for him? Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) was asked about the like of this and permitted it, citing the report of the Khathami woman. So the aged man and the aged woman who have despaired of being able to perform Hajj may each equip someone to perform Hajj on their behalf, and it suffices. But one who is able to make the journey is not discharged by another; he must go out and perform Hajj himself, whether he is able in ease or not, and even if he fears an enemy, because he is in the state of one who may hope for that fear to pass and for the way to Hajj to open, and there is no fixed time appointed for Hajj.

Hajj is an obligation once in a lifetime. As long as a person still hopes to be able to perform it, the obligation remains upon him; and if he finds a way to it at last and yet delays, he has wronged himself.

Hajj may be performed on behalf of one who has died, whether the deceased bequeathed it or his guardian volunteers to equip someone to perform it for him. If the deceased bequeathed that Hajj be performed on his behalf from the third of his estate, it is taken from that third. If he did not specify the third and had not yet performed his obligatory Hajj, it is taken from the whole of his estate, and any further bequests he made after that are paid from the third.

Whoever is engaged to perform Hajj on behalf of another, and finds that the wage exceeds his expenses, may keep the surplus, and the Hajj is credited both to him and to the one on whose behalf he performs it. One who has not yet performed Hajj for himself is only a hired man in this; if he has already performed his own Hajj, that is better. A man may perform Hajj on behalf of a man, and a woman on behalf of a woman. If a woman performs Hajj on behalf of a man, it suffices him when he can find no other, or when she is more capable than the men available to him and more exact in performing the rites. Whoever performs Hajj on behalf of another should strive to complete the Hajj in full and to discharge all its rites.

It was narrated of Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) that, after his son Ismail (ع) died, he hired a man to perform Hajj on his behalf, instructed him in what to do during the Hajj, and stipulated its conditions upon him. Then he said to him: "Know that if you fulfill what we have stipulated of you, it will count as a Hajj for the one on whose behalf you have performed it, and you will have a reward for keeping the condition laid upon you and for the labor of your body." And the Messenger of Allah (ص) said that Allah, mighty and majestic, admits three into Paradise on account of a single Hajj: the one who bequeaths that Hajj be performed for him, the one who carries out his bequest after him, and the pilgrim who performs it on his behalf, if he strives and fulfills the duty upon him.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (ع) said that there is no harm if one who performs Hajj for another for a wage should add, on his own behalf as a volunteer, whatever circumambulation or Umrah he wishes, once he has discharged what he was engaged to do. He also said (ع): whoever performs Hajj on behalf of another, let him say from the moment of his ihram, "اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أُرِيدُ الْحَجَّ عَنْ فُلَانٍ فَتَقَبَّلْ مِنْهُ وَأْجِرْنِي عَلَى قَضَائِي عَنْهُ" — O God, I intend the Hajj on behalf of so-and-so; accept it from him and reward me for discharging it on his behalf. Let him hold this intention and pronounce it at every station, at every sacred site and landmark, and in every act among the acts of Hajj, whether obligatory or recommended.

**Missed Hajj and Umrah**

Whoever performs the Hajj of tamattu, joining Umrah to Hajj, or the Hajj of qiran, and does not reach Mecca until a time when he fears that performing the circumambulation and the running of his Umrah would cause him to miss the standing, let him hasten instead to the standing so that his Hajj may be completed, make it a single Hajj, and perform the Umrah afresh afterward.

Whoever comes upon the people after they have left Mina and are standing at Arafat, and reaches the standing at Arafat before the sun sets, has attained the Hajj, even if he did not pass the night at Mina. Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said: likewise, if he reaches Arafat after the people have already poured forth from it, stands there through the night and remembers Allah, then comes to Jam before the people pour forth from Muzdalifah, he has attained the Hajj. But if he does not reach Muzdalifah until after the people have poured forth from it and the sun has risen, he has missed the Hajj.

One who has missed the Hajj should convert his ihram into Umrah, and the Hajj remains due from him for a future occasion, unless at the time of his ihram he stipulated that his release would be wherever he is prevented, in which case no Hajj is due from him for the missed occasion. Even then, Hajj remains upon him if he is one who has not yet performed his obligatory Hajj though he was able to find the way. Likewise, if he does not catch the people until after the days of Hajj have passed, let him circumambulate the House and make it a single Umrah, if he had been performing qiran or tamattu. But if he had entered ihram for Hajj alone, he owes no Umrah, because he neither entered ihram for Umrah nor intended it, unless he returns to the miqat and enters ihram for it there.

**The Vow of Hajj**

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "عَيْنًا يَشْرَبُ بِهَا عِبَادُ اللَّهِ يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا ۝ يُوفُونَ بِالنَّذْرِ وَيَخَافُونَ يَوْمًا كَانَ شَرُّهُ مُسْتَطِيرًا" — A fountain from which the servants of Allah drink, making it gush forth abundantly; they fulfill their vows and fear a Day whose evil is far-reaching [Al-Insan: 6-7]. We shall set out in the chapters on vows what of them is binding and what is not, God willing.

Whoever makes a binding vow to perform Hajj must fulfill it; and if he had not yet performed his obligatory Hajj, it suffices him in place of the Hajj of Islam. Abu Abdillah Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said that if he intends this and pronounces it, it is credited to him. Likewise, if he performs Hajj on behalf of another while he had also vowed to perform Hajj, that fulfills his vow and is credited to him.

It was narrated of Ali (ع) that he said: "Whoever vows to perform Hajj and is then unable to do so, let him send his sacrificial animal and enter ihram, remaining in the state of ihram among his household until it is sacrificed on his behalf." And Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said of one who makes a binding vow to walk to the Sacred House of Allah: let him walk; and when he grows weary and can no longer walk, let him ride and offer a sacrificial animal, for Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. When he has given the full measure of his effort, nothing further is upon him. A binding vow is one made in obedience; but whoever vows to commit a sin has nothing binding upon him.
